plain: Does every infinite space have a small, countable-sized shadow? The answer depends on the rules of set theory

object.heading: Must every infinite-dimensional Banach space have a separable quotient?

beats.text: Separable subspaces always exist. Quotients: open since at least Rosenthal, 1969
Under CH: a space of density $\aleph_1$ with no separable quotient. This half is in Lean
If $\mathfrak c$ is real-valued measurable, every space has one. That half is paper only

steps: Under CH, build a space from a tree indexed by countable ordinals
Its path functionals leave no room for a small quotient
With a measurable continuum instead, every space has one

statement: \mathfrak c \text{ real-valued measurable} \Rightarrow \text{every space has one}
achievement.context: Before: yes for separable spaces (1972) and for duals (2008); no counterexample in any model
achievement.note: Independence is relative to the consistency of a measurable cardinal

voice.text: Small subspaces always exist. Small quotients? Under one axiom, no; under another, always yes.
Under the continuum hypothesis, a tree-built space has no small quotient at all.
Claimed: independent, given a measurable cardinal.

sources.quote: Johnson and Rosenthal answered it for separable spaces in 1972, and Argyros, Dodos and Kanellopoulos for duals in 2008.

sources.ref: article, The separable quotient problem is independent of ZFC
sources.quote: Under the continuum hypothesis there is a counterexample of density $\aleph_1$. So, assuming a measurable cardinal is consistent, the problem is independent of ZFC.
The general problem was open; no counterexample was known in any model.
